core: What a referral is: a request that a second organization admit a person into its own rule system, and the four independent conditions (existence, capacity, eligibility, access) that must hold for it to produce a service

The resource landscape: public benefit programs, nonprofits, faith-based and mutual-aid organizations, health systems, and informal supports, and how funding structure, eligibility rules and geography determine what is obtainable

Information-and-referral infrastructure: the FCC's 2000 assignment of 211, the local-call-center structure of the 211 network, ZIP-scoped resource databases and taxonomies, and program-specific referral lines
Resource knowledge as maintained professional infrastructure rather than a static personal list
Evidence on referral completion: 211 follow-up outcomes, the Accountable Health Communities randomized comparison, and the risk-of-bias limits of the screening-and-referral literature
The referral intensity gradient from bare phone number to warm handoff to accompaniment, and what trial evidence shows a warm handoff does and does not change
Consent as a precondition when a referral moves identifiable records, including the 42 CFR 2.32 notice requirement for substance use disorder records
Matching the referral to the person's actual constraints: transportation, hours, documentation, language, disability access, cost, and immigration-related fear
Following up and closing the loop, including documenting the referral, its rationale, and its result
Structural honesty: what to do when the needed resource is absent, full, or closed, and why treating referral as a complete response to unmet need is a failure mode
supporting: Medicaid's transportation assurance at 42 CFR 431.53 as an example of a benefit that unlocks access to other services
Housing Choice Voucher waiting-list rules at 24 CFR 982.204 and 982.206 as a concrete instance of structural rationing
The volatility of federal public charge rules as an illustration of why practitioners describe rules and refer to counsel rather than advising
NASW case management standards on knowledge maintenance, cultural and linguistic access, documentation of referrals, and advocacy when resource gaps recur
outOfScope: The case management cycle, its phases, and the brokerage/clinical/strengths/ACT model taxonomy (owned by what-case-management-is)
HIPAA structure, authorization elements, 42 CFR Part 2 in detail, mandated reporting and duty-to-protect (owned by confidentiality-and-privacy)
Assessment method, screening instruments, and how needs are identified (owned by needs-assessment)
Systems change, policy advocacy method, community organizing, and coalition building (owned by advocacy and community-practice)
Any individualized guidance about whether a specific person qualifies for a specific benefit, or any immigration, legal, or clinical direction
Current dollar eligibility thresholds for any program

claims.claim: In its Third Report and Order adopted 21 July 2000 (FCC 00-256), the Federal Communications Commission granted a petition by the Alliance of Information and Referral Systems, United Way of America and several state information-and-referral networks and assigned the three-digit code 211 for access to community information and referral services, reasoning that people faced urgent needs not addressed by 911 emergency service or the non-emergency police code 311.

The 211 service is delivered by a network of local and state call centers rather than a single national agency; United Way reported more than 200 such agencies and stated that the network responds to more than 13 million requests a year and made more than 19 million connections in 2025.

Each 211 center maintains a resource database of government, nonprofit and faith-based providers with eligibility information, application procedures and service locations; researchers working with 211 records describe a taxonomy of more than 10,000 categories and subcategories, with referrals matched to the caller's ZIP code, so that the availability of a referral varies geographically within a single state.

In a one-month follow-up of a random sample of 1,235 Missouri adults who called 2-1-1, 93 percent remembered receiving referrals, 91 percent of those attempted at least one, and 82 percent of those reached at least one referral, but only 36 percent of those who reached a referral received assistance; the two most common reasons for not receiving assistance were that the agency had no funds (34 percent) and that the caller did not qualify (25 percent). Assistance rates ranged from 67 percent for food to 17 percent for housing, with 35 percent for utilities and 25 percent for rent or mortgage.

An analysis of 711,613 requests across 50 social need categories received by 211 centers in seven states during 2018 measured 'system capacity', defined as the proportion of requests for which a referral could be provided at all; in Missouri that year capacity was 92 percent for food pantries but 39 percent for rent assistance and 26 percent for automobile assistance, varied by ZIP code, and varied seasonally for a few needs. The authors state explicitly that system capacity is an upper bound and is not the same as receiving assistance.

The federal Accountable Health Communities Model, which ran from 2017 until April 2023 with 28 bridge organizations, screened more than one million Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries for five core needs (housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility difficulties and interpersonal violence); 37 percent screened positive for at least one and 18 percent were also navigation-eligible.

In the Accountable Health Communities randomized Assistance Track comparison, beneficiaries offered navigation had rates of need resolution about six months after screening similar to those of the control group, which received a community referral summary without a navigation offer; the associated survey study reported that navigation did not significantly increase the rate of connection to community service providers or the rate of need resolution, and that when connections were made the resources were often insufficient to resolve the need.

The final Accountable Health Communities evaluation reports that some participating communities did not have resources sufficient to meet demand for services addressing core needs, and that navigators had difficulty tracking which community-based organizations had capacity to accept new people.

In a randomized trial of hospitalized smokers, a bedside warm handoff in which staff called the quitline from the room and handed the patient the phone produced quitline enrollment of 99.6 percent versus 59.6 percent for fax referral sent at discharge, while biochemically verified abstinence at six months was about 25 percent in both arms and did not differ significantly; hospital-borne costs were significantly lower for warm handoff than for fax referral.

A warm handoff is described in the integrated-care literature as a referral approach in which the referring clinician directly introduces the person to the receiving provider in a face-to-face encounter at the time of the visit, with the aim of establishing a working alliance with the new provider.

A 2021 systematic review of 35 studies of screening-and-referral care delivery models found reported improvements in experience-of-care, population-health and cost outcomes, but judged all but one of the included studies to show a tendency toward high risk of bias, so no definitive conclusion about overall impact could be drawn; in five studies, outcomes were better for participants who received direct referrals or additional assistance than for those receiving indirect referrals only.

Federal rental assistance is structurally rationed rather than open-ended: under 24 CFR 982.204 a public housing agency must select participants from a waiting list in accordance with its written admission policies, must record each applicant's qualification for any local preference, and may not skip the family at the top of the list when funds are insufficient for that family's unit size; under 24 CFR 982.206 the agency may stop accepting new applications when the existing list contains an adequate pool for available program funding.

Transportation is sometimes itself an arrangeable benefit rather than a fixed barrier: 42 CFR 431.53 requires a State Medicaid plan to specify that the agency will ensure necessary transportation for beneficiaries to and from providers, and to describe the methods used to meet that requirement.

When a referral moves identifiable substance use disorder treatment records, federal law attaches restrictions that travel with the record: under 42 CFR 2.32 each disclosure made with the patient's written consent must be accompanied by a written statement notifying the recipient of limits on further use and disclosure of the record.

Rules that determine the consequences of using benefits can change quickly, which is a reason practitioners describe current published rules and refer people to counsel rather than advising them: the public charge regulation at 8 CFR 212.22, still shown as current in the eCFR text dated 14 August 2026, was the subject of a Department of Homeland Security final rule published 20 July 2026 (91 FR 45324) rescinding the 2022 public charge regulations effective 18 September 2026.

Professional case management standards treat knowledge of service delivery systems as something the practitioner must acquire and actively maintain, require documentation of referrals together with the rationale for them, direct the practitioner to notify a client promptly when a service will be interrupted or terminated by a provider and to make the necessary transfer or referral for continuity, and state that under resource scarcity the practitioner should still inform the client of the full range of existing choices, with recurring resource gaps calling for program development, community organizing, or policy and legislative advocacy.

Referral infrastructure is not limited to 211: the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program directs people to a National Energy Assistance Referral line and a locator site for local application information, while 988, designated by Congress in 2020 and operated through the existing National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, provides 24/7 crisis support rather than community-service referral.

Front-line information-and-referral staff themselves report that community resources are inadequate for some categories of need: in a survey of 471 information-and-referral specialists, resource managers and call center directors from 44 states, Puerto Rico and Canada, more than half rated community resources inadequate across all child care dimensions asked about.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does adding a navigator or warm handoff improve outcomes, or only improve connection?
positions: The Richter 2016 randomized trial found a very large improvement in the process outcome (quitline enrollment, 99.6 percent versus 59.6 percent) with no difference in the health outcome at six months.

The Accountable Health Communities evaluation found no significant navigation effect on connection or need resolution in the randomized comparison, yet did find reductions in expenditures and hospital-based utilization, and offers several possible mechanisms (trust with navigators, appointment support, partial resolution of needs, subgroup effects).
A 2021 systematic review reported generally positive findings for screening-and-referral models but judged nearly all included studies at high risk of bias.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson reports these as they stand rather than resolving them: intensity reliably improves connection, connection is not equivalent to resolution, and the effectiveness literature is not strong enough to support confident claims about what fixes referral completion. No causal claim about outcomes is made from the AHC design, whose Alignment Track was not randomized and whose Assistance Track outcome findings sit alongside a null connection finding.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How much can be claimed from the warm-handoff literature more broadly?
positions: The 2023 telehealth warm-handoff study is a randomized vignette study measuring anticipated likelihood of accepting and continuing treatment, not actual attendance.
The 2016 quitline trial measured actual enrollment and biochemically verified abstinence.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The vignette study is cited only for the definition and rationale of a warm handoff, never for effect size; the quantitative claim in the lesson rests on the quitline trial, and its limits are stated in the lesson text.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How current is the 211 coverage figure?
positions: A 2016 study describes 270 call centers covering more than 90 percent of the US population and 15.6 million calls in 2013.
United Way's own 2026 page reports more than 200 agencies, more than 13 million requests a year, and more than 19 million connections in 2025.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses only the 2026 self-reported agency count, explicitly attributed and dated, and does not state a national coverage percentage, since the two sources differ and neither is an independent current audit.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's assertion that the topic is 'a foundational concept' that students use 'to organize information, ask better questions, and explain relationships' - content-free boilerplate with no referral-practice substance.

The draft's framing of the topic as a definition to be recognized and applied to 'a simple scenario', which misrepresents referral as a conceptual exercise rather than a procedure with measurable completion rates.
The draft's map-legend and toolbox-drawer analogies, which carry no information about how referrals succeed or fail.
The draft's vocabulary entries ('context', 'evidence', 'application'), which are generic study-skills terms rather than terms of art in this topic.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the entire generated draft with researched content; no draft wording survives.
Added the empirical core the draft lacked: referral completion rates, the reasons referrals fail, and system-capacity data by need type.

Added the structural-honesty section stating that many needs cannot be met by referral because the resource is absent, full, or restricted, and that treating referral as a complete response is a failure mode.
Added the consent precondition for referrals that move records, with a pointer to the confidentiality lesson rather than re-teaching it.
Dated every quantitative figure to its study year and jurisdiction, and stated no current eligibility thresholds for any program.
Added an explicit educational-material statement and a rule-volatility warning anchored to a live example (the July 2026 public charge rescission rule).
rightsIssues: NASW Standards for Social Work Case Management (2013) is copyrighted; it is used REFERENCE_ONLY, read via local PDF text extraction, and every use in the lesson is restated in original wording with no reproduction of standard text.

The Health Affairs, Journal of Social Service Research, American Journal of Preventive Medicine and Journal of Child Health Care articles are copyrighted; they are used REFERENCE_ONLY for facts and figures only, with no wording reused. Two of them (Richter 2016, Renaud 2023, Thompson 2018) were read at abstract level via the Europe PMC API, which is noted in their source records.
United Way's 211 page is a self-published organizational source; its figures are attributed to United Way and dated rather than presented as independent measurements.

Federal regulations, the FCC order, CMS evaluation reports, ACF and SAMHSA pages are U.S. government works and are treated as public domain; the JMIR Formative Research and Preventing Chronic Disease articles are CC BY and require attribution, which is given, though no wording is reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Third Report and Order and Order on Reconsideration, In the Matter of the Use of N11 Codes and Other Abbreviated Dialing Arrangements (FCC 00-256, CC Docket No. 92-105)
sourceRecords.provider: Federal Communications Commission
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal agency order; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Primary source for the 211 assignment. Adopted 21 July 2000, released 31 July 2000. Paragraphs 17-20 read in full via local PDF text extraction: the petition by the Alliance of Information and Referral Systems, United Way of America, United Way 211 (Atlanta), United Way of Connecticut, the Florida Alliance of Information and Referral Services and the Texas I&R Network; the Commission's finding of sufficient public benefit; the assignment of 211 for access to community information and referral services; and its reasoning that these needs are not addressed by 911 or by the non-emergency police code 311. Also supports the observation that 211 was operating unevenly by state in 2000. Used for the historical claim only, not for current coverage.

sourceRecords.title: Getting help from 2-1-1: A statewide study of referral outcomes
sourceRecords.provider: Boyum S, Kreuter MW, McQueen A, Thompson T, Greer R; Journal of Social Service Research 42(3):402-411; author manuscript on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on PMC. The central referral-completion evidence in the lesson: random sample of 1,235 adult Missouri 2-1-1 callers followed at one month; 93 percent remembered referrals, 91 percent of those attempted contact, 82 percent of those reached a referral, 36 percent of those who reached one received assistance; reasons for non-assistance (agency had no funds 34 percent, caller did not qualify 25 percent); assistance by need (food 67, utilities 35, rent/mortgage 25, housing 17 percent); problem resolution roughly half at one month. Also supports the description of 211 resource databases containing eligibility information, application procedures and service locations for government, nonprofit and faith-based organizations, and the note that about half of 211s are operated through United Way. Data collected 2010-2012; used as dated evidence, not as a current national figure.

sourceRecords.title: Assessing The Capacity Of Local Social Services Agencies To Respond To Referrals From Health Care Providers
sourceRecords.provider: Kreuter M, Garg R, Thompson T, McQueen A, Javed I, Golla B, Caburnay C, Greer R; Health Affairs 39(4):679-688; author manuscript on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on PMC. Supports the system-capacity concept and its explicit limits, the 2018 seven-state dataset of 711,613 requests across 50 need categories, the Missouri capacity figures used in the lesson (food pantries 92, rent assistance 39, automobile assistance 26 percent), ZIP-code and seasonal variation, the 10,000-plus category taxonomy, the ZIP-scoped referral process and the definition of an 'unmet' request (no agency serving that ZIP code, or no resources currently available). Also the authors' statement that capacity is an upper bound and that the share who actually receive assistance is much lower, citing the 2016 statewide follow-up study.

sourceRecords.title: Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model Evaluation: Executive Summary for the Final Report
sourceRecords.provider: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Center for Medicare & Medicaid Innovation, and RTI International
sourceRecords.notes: Seven-page PDF read in full via local text extraction. Supports the model description (launched 2017, ended April 2023, 28 bridge organizations, universal screening for five core needs, universal referral, navigation offered to those with a need and two or more prior ED visits), the screening figures (more than one million beneficiaries screened, 37 percent positive for at least one core need, 18 percent navigation-eligible), the randomized Assistance Track design, the finding that need resolution about six months after screening was similar between intervention and control groups, the statement that evidence was mixed on whether navigation connected and resolved better than referral alone, and the findings that some communities lacked sufficient resources and that navigators had trouble tracking community-based organization capacity. Expenditure and utilization findings were read but are not used in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: Accountable Health Communities Model
sourceRecords.provider: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Center for Medicare & Medicaid Innovation
sourceRecords.notes: Model landing page read in full. Supports the model's structure (screening, referral, navigation, and alignment of community capacity), the Assistance and Alignment tracks, the 28 participating bridge organizations as of April 2022, the model performance period of 1 May 2017 to 30 April 2023, and the explicit statement that model funds supported bridge organization infrastructure and staffing and did not pay for the community services themselves - which matters for reading the null connection findings.

sourceRecords.title: Addressing Health-Related Social Needs Via Community Resources: Lessons From Accountable Health Communities
sourceRecords.provider: Renaud J, McClellan SR, DePriest K, et al.; Health Affairs 42(6):832-840
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 37196207); full text is paywalled and was not obtained. Supports the finding that navigation did not significantly increase the rate of community service provider connections or the rate of need resolution relative to the randomized control group, and that when connections were made resources were often insufficient to resolve the need. Used only for those two findings, which the CMS final evaluation executive summary independently corroborates and cites.

sourceRecords.title: Warm Handoff Versus Fax Referral for Linking Hospitalized Smokers to Quitlines
sourceRecords.provider: Richter KP, Faseru B, Shireman TI, et al.; American Journal of Preventive Medicine 51(4):587-596; author manuscript on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Structured abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 27647059). Individually randomized clinical trial in two Midwestern hospitals, recruitment from July 2011. Supports the lesson's central warm-handoff figures: quitline enrollment 99.6 percent for bedside warm handoff versus 59.6 percent for fax referral (relative risk 1.67), biochemically verified abstinence at six months 25.4 versus 25.3 percent with no significant difference, and significantly lower hospital-borne costs for warm handoff. Used for the process-versus-outcome contrast, not as evidence that warm handoffs improve health outcomes.

sourceRecords.title: Examining the Utility of a Telehealth Warm Handoff in Integrated Primary Care for Improving Patient Engagement in Mental Health Treatment: Randomized Video Vignette Study
sourceRecords.provider: Fountaine AR, Iyar MM, Lutes LD; JMIR Formative Research, 2023; on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Full text read on PMC. Used only for the definition and rationale of a warm handoff - a referral approach in which the referring clinician directly introduces the patient to the receiving mental health provider in a face-to-face encounter at the time of the visit, aimed at establishing a working alliance with the new provider. The study's own effect estimates are not used in the lesson because, as its limitations section states, it measured behavioral intent in a hypothetical video vignette rather than actual uptake, in a convenience sample of undergraduates. No wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Screening and Referral Care Delivery Services and Unmet Health-Related Social Needs: A Systematic Review
sourceRecords.provider: Ruiz Escobar E, Pathak S, Blanchard CM; Preventing Chronic Disease 18:E78 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 34387188). Supports the lesson's statement about the state of the evidence: 35 studies met inclusion criteria, all but one showed a tendency toward high risk of bias, improvements were reported across experience-of-care, population-health and cost outcomes but no definitive conclusion on overall impact was possible, and in five studies outcomes were better for participants receiving direct referrals or additional assistance than for those receiving indirect referrals only.

sourceRecords.title: 24 CFR 982.204 - Waiting list: Administration of waiting list
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development; Code of Federal Regulations, read via Cornell Legal Information Institute
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal regulation; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Section read in full. Supports the lesson's structural-rationing example: except for special admissions, participants must be selected from the PHA waiting list in accordance with the admission policies in the PHA Administrative Plan; the list must record each applicant's date and time of application and qualification for any local preference; and where funds are insufficient to subsidize the family unit size of the family at the top of the list, the PHA may not skip that family to admit a smaller one. Used to show that eligibility and receipt are distinct, not to describe any program's current eligibility thresholds.

sourceRecords.title: 24 CFR 982.206 - Waiting list: Opening and closing; public notice
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development; Code of Federal Regulations, read via Cornell Legal Information Institute
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal regulation; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Section read in full. Supports the closed-waiting-list case used in the lesson and in question 5: if the PHA determines that the existing waiting list contains an adequate pool for use of available program funding, it may stop accepting new applications or accept only applications meeting criteria it adopts. Also supports the public-notice requirements when a list is opened.

sourceRecords.title: 42 CFR 431.53 - Assurance of transportation
sourceRecords.provider: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services; Code of Federal Regulations, read via Cornell Legal Information Institute
sourceRecords.license: U.S. federal regulation; edict of government, not subject to copyright
sourceRecords.notes: Section read in full. Supports the lesson's point that transportation is sometimes an arrangeable benefit rather than a fixed barrier: a State Medicaid plan must specify that the agency will ensure necessary transportation for beneficiaries to and from providers, and must describe the methods used to meet that requirement. sourceRecords.title: 8 CFR 212.22 - Public charge inadmissibility determination

sourceRecords.title: Public Charge Ground of Inadmissibility (final rule, 91 FR 45324)
sourceRecords.provider: U.S. Department of Homeland Security; Federal Register

sourceRecords.title: NASW Standards for Social Work Case Management (2013)
sourceRecords.provider: National Association of Social Workers
sourceRecords.notes: Reused source record; read again via local PDF text extraction for this topic. Supports, in original restatement only: Standard 1's direction that under organizational or community resource scarcity the practitioner should still inform the client of the full range of existing choices, and that unresolved conflicts and recurring resource gaps call for program development, community organizing, or policy and legislative advocacy; the ethical duties to notify the client promptly when a service will be interrupted or terminated by a provider and to make the necessary transfer or referral for continuity; Standard 3's requirement to acquire and maintain knowledge of service delivery systems and to seek consultation when a situation falls outside the worker's usual setting; Standard 4 on culturally and linguistically appropriate access, including language preference and proficiency; Standard 6 on planning, implementing and monitoring services; Standard 7 on advocacy for access to resources; and the record-keeping element requiring referrals to be documented with their rationale and outcomes. sourceRecords.title: About Us - United Way 211
sourceRecords.provider: United Way Worldwide
sourceRecords.notes: Organizational self-description read in full on 18 August 2026. sourceRecords.title: Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP)
sourceRecords.provider: Office of Community Services, Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services

sourceRecords.title: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline
sourceRecords.provider: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
sourceRecords.notes: Page read in full. Supports the compare-and-contrast claim distinguishing 988 from 211: Congress designated the 988 dialing code in 2020, to be operated through the existing National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, and it offers 24/7 support by call, text or chat for mental health and substance use crises. sourceRecords.title: What would help low-income families? Results from a North American survey of 2-1-1 helpline professionals
sourceRecords.provider: Thompson T, Roux AM, Kohl PL, Boyum S, Kreuter MW; Journal of Child Health Care 22(4):670-683; author manuscript on PubMed Central
sourceRecords.notes: Abstract read via the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 29788775). Supports the supporting claim that information-and-referral staff themselves judge community resources inadequate for some need categories: 471 information and referral specialists, resource managers and call center directors from 44 states, Puerto Rico and Canada were surveyed, and across all child care dimensions asked about, more than half rated community resources inadequate. Used as corroboration of the scarcity theme only; the survey's ranking of which needs matter most is not used.
